author_response_spans.text: ## **Reply to the first Reviewer’s report:**
**Comment 1:** _The authors should ensure that all abbreviations are defined at their first appearance to prevent reader confusion._
**Authors Reply:** As requested, we have thoroughly checked the manuscript from the beginning to the end and all abbreviations have been defined at their first appearance.

**Comment 2:** _Could the authors elucidate the observed changes in the mass fraction of Ag before and after SPS for varying sintering durations, given the sintering temperature is well below the melting points of Ag and Ag2Se? An explanation of Ag loss in the Ag2.3Se sample under these conditions would be valuable._
**Authors Reply:** Firstly, it should be mentioned that the sintering duration in this work does not have a notable impact on the total content of Ag element in the material,

but it has a remarkable effect on the mass fraction of metallic Ag and  Ag-rich nanoprecipitates in the films. As we elaborated in the manuscript, when the sintering temperature is higher than the phase transition temperature of Ag2Se (133°C) but lower than the melting points of either Ag or Ag2Se, Ag2Se undergoes a transformation from an orthorhombic phase ( _β_ -Ag2Se) to a fast-ion conductor with cubic phase ( _α_ -Ag2Se), [8-9] which may enable the migration of Ag+ ions from metallic Ag into Ag-rich nanoprecipitates. For example, the cross-sectional morphology of Ag/Ag2Se film changes little when the sintering temperature is below the phase transition temperature (Fig. R1a and Fig. R1b). However, when the sinter temperature is higher than the phase transition temperature, such as 140°C, and sintering duration is 1 min, the morphology of Ag/Ag2Se film changes rapidly (Fig. R1c), and the mass fraction of metallic Ag in the sintered film is reduced from 7.84% to 4.39% ( **Supplementary Table 2** ). Another example is that when the sinter temperature is 200°C and sintering durations are 5 min, the mass fraction of metallic Ag in this sintered film continuously drops to 4.06%, and the mass fraction of Ag-rich nanoprecipitates in this sample is 27% ( **Supplementary Table 4** ).

**Comment 3:** _Including a schematic of the measurement circuit and a comprehensive procedural description would enhance clarity._

**Authors Reply:** As requested, the schematic of measurement circuit is added, which is displayed in Fig. R2, and this figure has also been added into _**Supporting Information**_ **as Supplementary Fig. 13** . For the measurement, the total length of the film is 10 mm. The silver pastes with a length of about 2mm were coated on both ends serving as electrodes. One electrode is attached to a heating plate, acting as the hot end. Another electrode is suspended, serving as the cold end. A resistor is connected in series with the film, and a multimeter is connected in parallel across the resistor. By varying the resistance of resistor and measuring the voltage drop across the resistor using the multimeter, the current through the resistor and the power of the resistor (represents the output power of the film) can be calculated. The actual temperatures of the hot and cold ends of the film are measured separately using two thermocouples of a temperature scanner.

**Comment 4:** _The section discussing the reversible trend in film length and Th lacks numerical data. Supporting this claim with quantitative evidence would strengthen the discussion._

**Authors Reply:** As shown in Fig. 5b and 5d in the original manuscript (the below Fig. R3b and R3c), we speculate that the “reversible trend in film length and Th” you mentioned refer to the values of maximum output power for the films, and not the temperatures of hot end ( _T_ h), that show the “reversible trend” in relation to the length of films. This trend emerges because the open circuit voltage (Uoc) of the film initially increases and then remains constant as the length of the film increases, whereas the internal resistance continuously rises with increasing length.

As we have described in the manuscript, a model has been constructed for the thermoelectric device fabricated in this work, wherein one end (hot side) is held at a fixed temperature ( _T_ h) while the other end (cold side) is subjected to natural convective conditions in air (shown in Fig. R3a). As displayed in Fig. R3b, with the _T_ h of 308.15 K, the  cold-end temperature ( _T_ c) gradually decreases from 306.45 K to 298.23 K as the length of the film increases. Corresponding, the open circuit voltage ( _U_ oc) increases from 0.19 mV to 1.14 mV, and the value of maximum output power reaches up to 1.40 μW when the length of film is 6 mm. In Fig. R3c, with the increasing length of film, the _T_ c drops from 314.76 K to 298.31 K for the _T_ h of 318.15 K. In addition, the _U_ oc climbs from 0.39 mV to 2.28 mV and a peak value for maximum output power of 5.58 μW is realized in the film. The related data and content have been added into the revised manuscript.

As shown in Fig. R4, the contact resistance between the silver paste (used as the electrodes) and thermoelectric film has been measured to be 3.92 mΩ employing a contact resistance testing system (PURI Materials, PR-CRM-01). This figure has been added into the revised _**Supporting Information**_ **as Supplementary Fig. 11** .

**Comment 7:** _The authors should present phase fractions of Ag₂Se and Ag based on EDS analysis for all samples. Clarification of the apparent inconsistencies in Table 3's phase composition is also necessary._

**Authors Reply:** EDS analysis is applied to determine the average atomic fractions of Ag and Se elements in the Ag-rich area and _β_ -Ag2Se matrix for composite powder and films in this work, and the revised results are shown in **Supplementary Table 1** (Table R1).

The phase compositions of the films exhibit notable differences depending on whether metallic Ag is present and whether Ag-rich nanoprecipitates form, thereby resulting in the “apparent inconsistencies” in the phase compositions.

Since the Ag-rich nanoprecipitates are transformed from metallic Ag, and there is no metallic Ag present in the Ag2.0Se-SPS200[o] C/5min film, this film only contains _β_ - Ag2Se. In addition, TEM images indicate that the Ag-rich nanoprecipitates with notable size can hardly be observed in Ag2.1Se-SPS200[o] C/5min film (revised **Supplementary Fig. 3a** ) and Ag2.3Se-SPS140[o] C/1min film ( **Fig. 2a in the manuscript** ), thus, these two films are composed of _β-_ Ag2Se and metallic Ag. The phase compositions of these two films have been determined with the results of Rietveld refined XRD patterns in the revised **Supplementary Fig. 5 and Supplementary Table 2.**

For Ag2.3Se-SPS200[o] C/5min film, Ag2.3Se-SPS200[o] C/30min film and Ag2.5SeSPS200[o] C/5min film which are composed of _β-_ Ag2Se matrix, metallic Ag and Ag-rich nanoprecipitates, the phase compositions are calculated with the revised results of Rietveld refined XRD patterns, ICP spectroscopy (revised **Supplementary Table 3)** and EDS analysis, using the method described in revised **Supplementary Note 1.** The revised phase compositions are displayed in the revised **Supplementary Table 4** (displayed in Table R2). It is noteworthy that, due to potential measurement errors associated with TEM-EDS and ICP analyses, as well as uncertainties from XRD refinement, the phase compositions of the composite films in this study can only be

**Comment 8:** _The manuscript should provide a detailed explanation of the nylon flexible substrate and glass fiber, elaborating on their roles and impact on the film’s performance._

**Authors Reply:** The schematic process for fabricating the nylon supported thermoelectric films in this work is added in _**Supporting Information**_ as **Supplementary Fig. 1** (Fig. R6). From this schematic diagram, it is easy to understand that the glass fiber membrane is merely an intermediate medium used for the preparation of nylon supported composite films rather than the component of the final nylon supported film, therefore, the glass fiber has no effect on the thermoelectric performance of the composite films. Moreover, given that the sintering temperature utilized in this work is merely 200°C, falling below both the melting point and decomposition temperature of nylon, it is impossible for decomposition products of

nylon to penetrate into the thermoelectric film. Consequently, the nylon film has no impact on the composition and performance of the thermoelectric film, which has also been confirmed in previous articles reported by our team and other groups.[ [11-14]]

## **Reply to the second Reviewer’s report:**
**Comment 1:** _What is your setup for experimentally measuring power? How much is its accuracy and what is the percentage of error?_

**Authors Reply:** The schematic diagram of measurement circuit is displayed in Fig. R7, and this figure has been added in _**Supporting Information**_ **as Supplementary Fig. 13.** The total length of the film is 10 mm, with 2 mm of silver paste coated on both ends serving as electrodes. One electrode is attached to a heating plate, acting as the hot end, while the other electrode is suspended, serving as the cold end. A resistor is connected in series with the film, and a digital multimeter is connected in parallel across the resistor. By varying the resistance of resistor and measuring the voltage drop across the resistor using the multimeter, the current through the resistor and the power of the resistor (represents the output power of the film) can be calculated. The actual temperatures of the hot and cold ends of the film are measured separately using two thermocouples of a temperature scanner.

The brand of multimeter used for measuring output voltage is Fluke (12E+), and according the manual, the error for this multimeter is ±0.5%. The brand of multiplex temperature meter is DCUU (DC5508U), and its error is ±0.1[o] C.
**Comment 2:** _How is the repeatability of the results? How many samples did you fabricate to show similar results?_

**Authors Reply:** Throughout the entire work period, using Ag2.3Se composite powder synthesized via the solvothermal reaction, tens of Ag2.3Se-SPS200[o] C/5min films and bulks have been prepared, with over 80% samples exhibiting a power factor exceeding 4000 μWm[-1] K[-2] . Moreover, some samples were subjected to comparative testing using equipment from different institutions (Guilin University of Electronic Technology and Shanghai Institute of Ceramics, Chinese Academy of Sciences). The difference in power factor amounted to only 2%, indicating the good reliability of thermoelectric data in this work.

The representative thermoelectric performance of 10 samples (films and bulks) are shown in Fig. R8. Given the systematic error of ZEM-3 for measuring the Seebeck coefficient and electrical conductivity are about 7 % and 10 %, respectively, the results of thermoelectric performance obtained in this work demonstrate a satisfactory level of reproducibility. This figure has been added in the revised _**Supporting Information**_ **as Supplementary Fig. 9** .

**Comment 3:** _You have measured density, Cp, and thermal diffusivity, but what is the thermal conductivity of Ag2.3Se sample? Knowing the thermal conductivity of the Ag2.3Se, how much is the zT? Also, what is your zT compared to literature?_

**Authors Reply:** Perhaps you may miss these data in our original manuscript, we have shown the data of  thermal conductivity and _ZT_ of Ag2.3Se sample in the manuscript, which are 1.77 Wm[-1] K[-1] and 0.7 at 303 K, respectively.

Wei’s group has summarized _ZT_ at or near room temperature of Ag2Se-based thermoelectric materials prepared by various methods,[ [15]] which is cited and displayed in the following Fig. R9. Consequently, the _ZT_ in this work resides within an aboveaverage level. It is worth emphasizing that the Ag2.3Se sample reported in this work exhibits an unprecedented power factor, leading to a higher output power density compared to other Ag2Se-based materials. This makes it highly suitable for powering
wearable electronic devices.

**Comment 5** : _The authors have shown the ratio of internal resistance before (R0) and after (R) bending. What is power and voltage before and after bending?_

**Authors Reply:** Because the voltage is directly proportional to the Seebeck coefficient of the film, in response to your inquiry, we have conducted the additional flexibility test to study the trend of changes in electrical conductivity and Seebeck coefficient of the films after undergoing bending cycles, and the results have placed in the revised **manuscript as Fig. 5g** (Fig. R11). After 800 bending cycles, an increase in resistivity ( _ρ_ b) of the bent film is observed, amounting to approximately a 10% elevation compared to its pristine resistivity ( _ρ_ 0), then no further increase is observed during the subsequent bending cycles. On the other hand, throughout the entire flexibility test, the variation in the Seebeck coefficient of the bent film ( _S_ b) remained within ±4% of its original value ( _S_ 0), suggesting that the bending cycles can hardly affect the Seebeck coefficient of the film. Therefore, the voltage can remain almost constant after bending, while the power is inversely proportional to resistivity.

and R13b). Here, please allow us to clarify these two figures again for you.

As described in our manuscript, to ascertain the optimal length of the device that yields maximum output power, a simulated model of the device in this work with a fixed hot-end temperature and a cold-end in a state of natural convention has been established ( **Fig. 5a in the revised manuscript** ). It is evident that the cold-end temperature gradually decreases as the length of the film increases, until a specific film length is reached where a thermal equilibrium is established between the heat conducted from the hot end to the cold end and the heat dissipated from the cold end through air convection. Even if the film length is further increased, the cold-end temperature will remain constant, matching the temperature of the surrounding air. Since the open circuit voltage is proportional to the temperature difference between the two ends of the film, the simulated open circuit voltage of the film gradually increases with the change in temperature of cold side and reaches a steady state, which you refer to “saturate at a length above 10”.

## **Reply to the third Reviewer’s report:**
**Comment 1:** _Introduction – 2nd paragraph_

_“Furthermore, owing to the extremely low solubility of most elements (including Ag and Se) in β-Ag2Se, the intrinsic small carrier concentration (nH) of stoichiometric β- Ag2Se can hardly be effectively elevated through doping or altering the Ag/Se ratio since the.”_
_What do you mean by low solubility? Please quantify._

**Authors Reply:** As reported by Conn et al.,[[1]] with the exception of Cu, AgI and the group IIB elements, doping agents had very little effect on Ag2Se. In many cases, the thermoelectric properties are identical for a particular element, at the doping levels of both 0.1 and 0.5 mole %, indicating that Ag2Se is saturated with respect to that element at <0.1 mole %. Thus, the doping limits of most elements are extremely low. We have added this value into the “ _**Introduction**_ ” and the “low solubility” is changed to “low doping limit”.
## **Reply to the Second Reviewer’s report:**

**Comments to the Authors:** _The authors have thoroughly answered most of the questions that has resulted in an improved manuscript. New figures, schematics, and data have clarified the claims in a good way. However, there are still concerns about the accuracy of the power and thermal conductivity._

**Authors Reply:** Thank you for the good comments. We have further elaborated on the issues of measurement in power and thermal conductivity, and we believe that this revised version will meet your specifications.

**Comment 1:** _When talking about the thermal conductivity of thin films, we need to be careful. As the authors may know, one of the main reasons that the research on thin film thermoelectrics is not mature is the complexity of thermal conductivity measurement. Spark plasma sintering of the same powder and measuring the bulk thermal conductivity data rather than thin film is barely accepted by thermoelectric experts, and it is generally not advisable to directly use bulk thermal conductivity values for thin films of the same compound, especially in thermoelectric applications. Thermoelectric performance is highly sensitive to thermal conductivity. Therefore, using inaccurate thermal conductivity values can lead to significant errors in device design and performance prediction. Thin films are manufactured in ways that create very different microstructures than bulk materials._
## **Authors Reply:**

We agree that the measurement of thermal conductivity for the films is quite challenging. Here we attempted to measure the Ag2.3Se-SPS200[o] C/5min films peeled from nylon substrates using the laser-flash apparatus (Netzsch LFA467), which is widely applied in thermoelectric research. The data are shown in Fig. R1. As the referee mentioned, a large deviation is observed because of the difficulty of measurement for thin films. If these data are used to calculate _zT_ , the values will reach up to1.5 or even exceed 2.3, which are obviously incorrect.

As far as we know, the electrical properties of Ag2Se-based materials are very sensitive to chemical compositions and microstructures ( _J. Phys. Chem. Lett._ 2021, 12, 8246−8255, _ACS Appl. Mater. Interfaces_ 2021, 13, 60192−60199), but the lattice thermal conductivity of Ag2Se is very low with the values of about 0.4~0.5 Wm[-1] K[-1] ( _J. Mater. Chem. A_ , 2020, 8, 13024, _Acta Materialia_ 2021, 220 _,_ 117335) which is not sensitive to the chemical compositions and microstructures. In this case, the deviation of total thermal conductivity should mainly come from the electronic contribution. As shown in Fig. R2, the electrical conductivity and Seebeck coefficient of the films in this work are close to those of the sintered bulk for Ag2.3Se-SPS200[o] C/5min. Therefore, we believe that the thermal conductivity of the film should be also similar as that in this bulk sample. In this case, a reasonable _zT_ of 0.7 is obtained.
In summary, the adoption of thermal conductivity of bulk in this work is justified, and the related discussions  have been added into the revised manuscript.

## Se Coherent Ag-rich nanoprecipitates/β-Ag2 flexible film with unprecedented thermoelectric performance by liquid-like sintering 

Received: 25 October 2024 Accepted: 12 June 2025 Check for updates 

Jie Gao 1, Jiahui Li1, Lei Miao 2 , Lida Jia[1] , Pengfei Qiu[3] , Tingwei Yin 3, Sijing Zhu 2, Xinyu Yang2, Jia-Chen Guo1, Jun-Liang Chen1, Xiaoyang Wang2, Eiji Nishibori 4, Tomohiro Sato5 & Xun Shi 3 

β-Ag2Se holds a great promise for wearable thermoelectric generators due to its good mechanical properties and biocompatibility. However, optimizing its power factor through alterations in the Ag/Se stoichiometric ratio or incorporating secondary phases has reached the limitation. This work adopts a liquid-like sintering strategy, namely employing the migration and precipitation of silver ions from metallic silver to the silver selenide during the spark plasma sintering process to construct significantly sized and coherent Ag-rich nanoprecipitates within flexible Ag/β-Ag2Se composite films, thereby achieving an unprecedented power factor exceeding 4000 μWm[−][1] K[−][2] at 303 K. The Ag-rich nanoprecipitates play a crucial role in elevating the carrier concentration, enhancing the density-of-states effective mass, and mitigating carrier scattering caused by phase interfaces and acoustic phonons. The generator containing 5 pieces of optimal films shows an normalized output power density of 10.89 μWcm[−][1] K[−][2] under a temperature difference of 26.0 K. This study strongly suggests that the creation of Ag-rich nanoprecipitates is an effective avenue for improving the electrical performance of β-Ag2Se-based thermoelectric materials.

The rapid progress in flexible electronics has catalyzed an exigent need for power sources adaptable to the inherent flexibility of these systems[1] . Flexible thermoelectric films, capable of conforming to the skin and continuously converting temperature difference between the human body and the ambient environment into electrical energy for flexible electronics, are viewed as a highly promising flexible selfpowered energy source[2][,][3] . Optimizing the power factor (PF) of the 

flexible thermoelectric film is the key to improving its output power density to meet the energy supply needs of as many electronic products as possible[4] . 

Due to its better mechanical properties and lower toxicity compared to the traditional BiTeSe alloys, N-type silver selenide (β-Ag2Se at room temperature) has attracted sharply increasing attention in the field of flexible thermoelectric films[5][,][6] . However, although its Hall

carrier mobility (μH) reaching up to 2000 cm[2] V[−][1] s[−][1] at room temperature, the values of density-of-states effective mass (md) for carriers in the stoichiometric β-Ag2Se are far smaller than that of BiTeSe alloys[7][–][9] . Furthermore, owing to the doping limits of most elements (including Ag and Se) in β-Ag2Se being less than 0.1 mole%, the intrinsic small carrier concentration (nH) of stoichiometric β-Ag2Se can hardly be effectively elevated through doping or altering the Ag/Se ratio since the 1960s[10][–][13] . Thus, the state-of-art values of PF for stoichiometric β- Ag2Se, in both bulk and film forms, typically remain below 2700 μWm[−][1] K[−][2] or even 2000 μWm[−][1] K[−][2] at around room temperature for decades, which is markedly inferior to the exceeding 4000 μWm[−][1] K[−][2] obtained by BiTeSe alloys[4][,][14][–][16] . On the other hand, despite incorporating metals or alloys as the second phase has been proven to enable the promotion of nH and enhancement of md in β- Ag2Se-based flexible films[17][,][18] , the values of PF for these films are still limited by the excessively high nH and additional carrier scattering at phase boundaries[19][–][22] . 

Very recently, we revealed that a previously overlooked microstructure, Ag-rich nanoprecipitates with a size of a few nanometers can be found in nominally stoichiometric β-Ag2Se sintered by spark plasma sintering (SPS)[23] . However, possibly because of their limited size and content, the nanoprecipitates did not exert a substantial influence on the thermoelectric properties of β-Ag2Se.

In this work, addressing the mobility of Ag ions and its low solubility in β-Ag2Se, a liquid-like SPS approach is proposed, wherein Ag ions migrate from metallic silver to silver selenide during the sintering process, subsequently bonding partially with selenium atoms and precipitating out to form Ag-rich nanoprecipitates with sizes reaching several tens of nanometers (marked with red arrows in Fig. 1d) in flexible Ag/β-Ag2Se film (see “Methods”, Supplementary Fig. 1 and Fig. 1a–d). As shown in Fig. 1e, the boundary between the Ag-rich nanoprecipitate and β-Ag2Se matrix is completely coherent due to their identical crystal structure of orthorhombic Ag2Se. The electrons transferred from the Ag-rich nanoprecipitates and metallic Ag to the β-Ag2Se matrix collectively pushed up the nH of composite films (see Supplementary Fig. 2), and the Ag-rich nanoprecipitates also play a significant role in enhancing the md and diminishing carrier scattering caused by phase interfaces and acoustic phonons. Thus, as depicted in Fig. 1f, despite a high nH of 22.16 × 10[18] cm[−][3] , this optimal film (named as Ag2.3Se-SPS200 °C/5 min) maintains a moderate μH of 855.4 cm[2] V[−][1] s[−][1] . Meanwhile, because of the appropriate nH and md, the optimal film retains a Seebeck coefficient of −116.3 μVK[−][1] , showing only a marginal decline compared to that of pristine β-Ag2Se (see Fig. 1g). As a result, via this novel strategy that can transform metallic Ag into the Ag-rich nanoprecipitates, an unprecedented PF exceeding 4000 μWm[−][1] K[−][2] has been achieved in the optimal film, setting a new benchmark for the electrical performance of β- Ag2Se based thermoelectric materials (see Fig. 1h).

In addition, regardless of whether the length of the film is taken into account, the normalized output power density (Pmd) of the thermoelectric generator formed by 5 pieces of optimal films (1 cm in length) significantly surpassing that of other β-Ag2Se based film-type thermoelectric generators (see Fig. 1i). 

## Results and discussion 

By systematically investigating the composition and microstructure of composite films fabricated from composite powders of varying compositions and subjected to different sintering processes, the potential formation mechanism of Ag-rich nanoprecipitates can be deduced. According to the molar ratio of AgNO3 to Se powder in the solvothermal reaction, and the temperature and duration of SPS, the obtained thermoelectric films are named as Ag2.0Se-SPS200 °C/5 min, Ag2.1SeSPS200 °C/5 min, Ag2.3Se-SPS140 °C/1 min, Ag2.3Se-SPS200 °C/5 min (the optimal film), Ag2.3Se-SPS200 °C/30 min, and Ag2.5Se-SPS200 °C/5 min. 

Since the Ag-rich nanoprecipitates with notable size in this work have never been reported in the stoichiometric β-Ag2Se, it is speculated 

that the presence of sufficient metallic Ag in the composite powder before sintering is a prerequisite for the formation of Ag-rich nanoprecipitates. High-angle annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADF-STEM) images in Supplementary Fig. 3 confirm this inference. In HAADF-STEM image of Ag2.1Se-SPS200 °C/5 min, hardly any notable Ag-rich nanoprecipitates can be observed, while HAADF-STEM images of Ag2.3Se-SPS200 °C/5 min and Ag2.5Se-SPS200 °C/5 min distinctly reveal the Ag-rich nanoprecipitates. 

Composition and microstructure of films fabricated using Ag2.3Se powder have been investigated to illustrate the formation process of Ag-rich nanoprecipitates.

For β-Ag2Se particles in the Ag2.3Se powder before sintering, the atomic fraction of Ag element is determined to be 67.69% by energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) maps (see Supplementary Fig. 4). As depicted in the dark-field TEM image presented in Fig. 2a, for Ag2.3Se-SPS140 °C/1 min film, numerous circular “bright” domains (typically marked with white arrows), primarily within 10 nm in size can be recognized by the strain field contrast. The result of EDS line scanning across a “bright” domain (see Supplementary Fig. 5) in Fig. 2d reveals that the average atomic fraction of Ag element in the “bright” domain (75.08%) is higher than that in the surrounding β-Ag2Se matrix (71.02%), namely, these domains are Agrich. Notably, the β-Ag2Se matrix also exhibits an elevated average atomic fraction of Ag element than that of the β-Ag2Se particles in the Ag2.3Se powder. For the composite films sintered at 200 °C for 5 min and 30 min, as shown in Fig. 2b, c, a large number of island-like nanoprecipitates spanning sizes from tens to approximately 100 nanometers can be observed. Determined by EDS maps of the typical nanoprecipitates (marked with red dashed lines) and β-Ag2Se matrix (marked with yellow dashed lines), for Ag2.3Se-SPS200 °C/5 min film, the average atomic fractions of Ag element in the nanoprecipitates and β-Ag2Se matrix are 69.42% and 67.15%, respectively. For clear comparison, the average atomic fractions of Ag element in the nanoprecipitates and β-Ag2Se matrix for all samples in this work are listed in Supplementary Table 1. As to Ag2.3Se-SPS200 °C/30 min film, the corresponding values increase to 73.49% and 68.81%, respectively. HRTEM images in Fig.

2e, f demonstrate that the boundaries between the Agrich nanoprecipitates and the surrounding matrix (indicated by red dashed lines) are coherent, and the Ag-rich nanoprecipitates exhibit pronounced Moiré fringes with varying spacings. The fast Fourier transform (FFT) patterns inserted in Fig. 2a, e, f, while displaying clear secondary diffraction features, can all be indexed to the orthorhombic phase of Ag2Se. 

Rietveld refined X-ray diffraction patterns have been employed to estimate the mass fraction of metallic Ag in the Ag2.3Se composite powder and the sintered films (see Supplementary Fig. 6 and Supplementary Table 2). All the diffraction peaks can be indexed to orthorhombic β-Ag2Se (JCPDF card number: 01-071-2410) and cubic metallic Ag (JCPDF card number: 03-065-2871), and Ag2.3Se composite powder contains approximately 8 wt% of metallic Ag. Nevertheless, as to the film sintered at 140 °C (slightly higher than the phase transition temperature (133 °C) of β-Ag2Se) for only 1 min, the Ag and Ag2Se particles quickly fused with each other to form bulks (see Supplementary Fig. 7), and the mass fraction of metallic Ag drops to about 4%. Further increasing the sintering temperature to 200 °C and extending the sintering durations to 5 and 30 min facilitated complete sintering of the composite films, which led to a reduction in the thickness of composite films and a shrinkage in size of the metallic Ag regions within the composite films (see Supplementary Figs. 8 and 9), but the mass fractions of metallic Ag in these films still remain around 4%. Hence, it is inferred that the excess Ag atoms in the Ag-rich nanoprecipitates stem from the metallic Ag, and the transfer of Ag atoms from metallic Ag to Ag2Se is completed during the phase transition.

## Fabrication of composite films and bulks 

The resulted powder was uniformly dispersed in 10 mL ethylene glycol and 1.2 mL of the dispersion was drop-casted on a piece of glass-fiber sheet with size of 5 mm × 20 mm. After the glass-fiber sheet coated with composite powder was dried in vacuum at 80 °C for 10 h, it was sandwiched between 2 pieces of nylon membrane and sintered at 30 MPa. During the sintering process, the composite powder was insulated from the pulse current of SPS equipment by the nylon membrane, avoiding the migration of Ag ions caused by the pulse current. The powder was transformed into the nylon-supported dense composite film during the sintering process, and the debris of glassfiber sheet could be easily removed with a brush. To demonstrate that the nylon substrate has no influence on the thermoelectric properties of the films, some composite bulk materials were also prepared by sintered the composite powder in the conditions same with the fabrication of films, but without using the glass-fiber membrane and nylon film.

## Material characterizations and property measurements 

The phase and composition of composite powders and films were analyzed by X-ray diffractometer using Cu Ka radiation (Rigaku, SmartLab). The mass fractions of Ag element and Se element in samples were acquired by inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectrometry (ICP-OES, Agilent 720). The morphology and thickness of composite powders and films were revealed via field emission scanning electron microscopy (Hitachi S-4800). The microstructures were observed by transmission electron microscopy (FEI TalosF200X), with an Oxford energy dispersive X-ray spectrometer (EDS) to analyze the elemental compositions and distributions of the samples. The simultaneous measurement of the Seebeck coefficient and electrical conductivity at room temperature were carried out in an Ulvac-Riko ZEM-3 system. The measurement was conducted in argon atmosphere with temperature gradients of 20, 30, and 40 °C. The carrier mobility and carrier concentration were collected using a Hall effect system (Lake Shore Cryotronics 8404). A laser flash diffusivity apparatus (Netzsch LFA 467) and a differential scanning calorimeter (Netzsch 404 F3) were applied to determine the thermal diffusivity and specific heat capacity, respectively. The density was measured via the Archimedes’ method. Since the measured thermal diffusivity of composite film is dramatically lower than the reasonable value, pellets were sintered using Ag/β-Ag2Se powder in the conditions same with the fabrication of films for the measurement of thermal diffusivity and density. Each pellet is circular, with a thickness of 0.5 mm and a diameter of 12.7 mm. The sound velocity was measured via a sound velocimeter (JSR, DPR300).

The hot and cold side temperatures of single composite film were measured employing a multiplex temperature meter (DCUU, DC5508U), with the cold side of film suspending in the air. The spot welding was used to connect Pt-Rh wires with the films, and the output properties of the thermoelectric generator composed of 5 pieces of films were collected by a multimeter (Agilent 34970A) and a constant current source (Agilent B2901A)[29] . The bending test was conducted via a hand-cranked tensile testing machine (AIGU, ZP-1000). 

## First-principles calculations 

This work utilized periodic slab models for all DFT calculations, conducted via the Vienna ab initio simulation package, including DFT-D3 empirical van der Waals corrections. The HSE exchange-correlation functional was applied within the generalized gradient approximation GGA[30] . Electron-ion interactions were described using the projectoraugmented wave method, employing a plane-wave basis set with a cutoff energy of 500 eV. A 3 × 4 × 3 Monkhorst-Pack k-point mesh for perfect bulk β-Ag2Se with lattice constants a = 9.17 Å, b = 7.04 Å, 

c = 7.58 Å. The coverage criteria for energies and forces were set to 10[−][5] eV and 0.02 eV/Å. The first order Methfessel–Paxton method with a smearing width of 0.05 eV was used. The model for the Ag-rich nanoprecipitate was constructed by removing one Se atom from the structure of Ag16Se8. For the (11-2) crystal plane of β-Ag2Se and its derived models, a 3 × 2 × 1 Monkhorst-Pack k-point mesh was applied. To calculate the deformation potential, the positions of the CBM for the structures with strain magnitudes ranging from −1% to 1% were calculated in increments of 0.5%. The energy difference between the CBM and the core energy level yields ECBM.

The slope of the variation of ECBM with strain represents the deformation potential of the material.

As the authors may know, one of the main reasons that the research on thin film thermoelectrics is not mature is the complexity of thermal conductivity measurement. Spark plasma sintering of the same powder and measuring the bulk thermal conductivity data rather than thin film is barely accepted by thermoelectric experts, and it is generally not advisable to directly use bulk thermal conductivity values for thin films of the same compound, especially in thermoelectric applications. Thermoelectric performance is highly sensitive to thermal conductivity. Therefore, using inaccurate thermal conductivity values can lead to significant errors in device design and performance prediction. Thin films are manufactured in ways that create very different microstructures than bulk materials.

It is suggested to use more robust multimeters such as the Keithley 2010 series. What sample did you use to calibrate your measurement? First, you need to calibrate your power measurement

system and then measure a new sample. The error of the multimeter is different from the error of the sample measurement. You need to know the estimated error of measurements. **Comments to the Authors:** _This manuscript, titled “Coherent Ag-rich Nanoprecipitates/β-Ag2Se Flexible Film with Unprecedented Thermoelectric Performance by Liquid-like Sintering,” presents an innovative approach to enhancing the thermoelectric performance of β-Ag2Se through a liquid-like sintering method, resulting in coherent Ag-rich nanoprecipitates in Ag/β-Ag2Se composite films. **Authors Reply:** Thank you for the good comments. Here, we would like to emphasize the novelty of this work. _β_ -Ag2Se is an excellent room-temperature thermoelectric material, which has been discovered for more than 60 years. However, its intrinsic maximum power factor is limited to below 2700 μWm[-1] K[-2 ] at room temperature in the bulk or film form. Moreover, the methods to optimize the power factor of _β_ -Ag2Sebased thermoelectric materials have been limited to adjusting the Ag/Se ratio and incorporating the second phase usually in the macro- or micro-scale, which are hard to improve the electrical properties greatly.[ [1-7]]

In this work, we try to use nanoscale Ag-rich precipitates to tune the thermoelectric properties of Ag2Se. By using spark plasma sintering, for the first time, the Ag-rich nanoprecipitates with sizes about tens of nanometers within the _β_ -Ag2Se matrix have been created. Ag-rich nanoprecipitates not only enhances the carrier concentration of the composites due to charge transfer effects, but also avoids additional carrier scattering, owing to the coherent boundaries between the Ag-rich nanoprecipitates and the _β_ -Ag2Se matrix. As a result, an unprecedented _PF_ exceeding 4000 μWm[-1] K[-2] at 303 K has been achieved in this work, which is far larger than the _β_ -Ag2Se matrix material. Therefore, we believe the strategy of using Ag nanoprecipitates to tune the properties of Ag2Se is new and the obtained ultrahigh power factors are breakthrough.

Secondly, during the drop-casting process, we apply the dispersion in a certain sequence (either from left to right or from right to left) across one end of the glass fiber membrane to the other, ensuring that each area of the glass fiber membrane surface receives an equal volume of the dispersion.
